summary: This informational memo describes Microsoft Point-to-Point Compression, a way to compress packets carried over PPP links. It documents a vendor method rather than an Internet standard.

plainLanguage.summary: MPPC is a way to shrink the packets sent over a PPP link. Both ends keep a copy of what has already been sent, so repeated text can be sent as a short pointer. A counter in every packet tells each end whether the two are still in step.

questions: how does mppc compress ppp packets
subtitle: Microsoft's compression scheme for PPP, and the packet format and rules that keep both ends in step.

tldr.problem: A link carrying many simultaneous connections benefits from compression, and the compressed form has to be agreed by both ends before it is used.
tldr.mechanism: MPPC compresses PPP packets with an LZ based algorithm and a sliding window history buffer of 8192 bytes. Each packet carries a 12 bit coherency count, and four flag bits say whether the history has just been flushed and whether the data is compressed.
tldr.outcome: The two ends stay in step through the coherency count, and a lost packet is recovered by a CCP Reset-Request that makes the sender flush its history. Licensing restricts MPPC to products that implement PPP and interoperate with other MPPC or PPP implementations.

today: RFC 2118 is an Informational memo from March 1997, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its licensing terms restrict MPPC to products that implement PPP and interoperate with other MPPC or PPP implementations, and its Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed in the memo.

sections.title: Introduction and Licensing
sections.content:
The Microsoft Point to Point Compression scheme is a means of representing arbitrary PPP packets in a compressed form. The MPPC algorithm is designed to optimize processor utilization and bandwidth utilization in order to support large numbers of simultaneous connections, and it is optimized to work efficiently in typical PPP scenarios such as a 1500 byte MTU. It uses an LZ based algorithm with a sliding window history buffer, and it keeps a continuous history so that after 8192 bytes of data has been transmitted compressed there is always 8192 bytes of history to use for compressing, except when the history is flushed.

Licensing is restricted. MPPC can only be used in products that implement PPP, and for the sole purpose of interoperating with other MPPC and PPP implementations. Source and object licenses are available on a non-discriminatory basis from Stac Electronics. The memo also sets out the meaning of the requirement words it uses: MUST and MUST NOT mark absolute requirements and absolute prohibitions, SHOULD marks an item that may be ignored for good reason if the implications are understood, and MAY marks one of a set of allowed alternatives.
sections.plainLanguage: The scheme keeps the last 8192 bytes of what was sent, so a repeat of something in that window can be sent as a short pointer back to it instead of the bytes themselves.

sections.title: Configuration Option
sections.content:
The CCP Configuration Option negotiates the use of MPPC on the link. By default, or on ultimate disagreement, no compression is used. The option carries a Type of 18 and a Length of 6, followed by a Supported Bits field.

The Supported Bits field is 4 octets, most significant octet first. The least significant bit in the least significant octet, set to 1, indicates a desire to negotiate MPPC, and all other bits must be set to 0.
sections.plainLanguage: Before any compressed packet is sent, the two ends agree over the same control protocol that other compression schemes use. The agreement is a single bit in a four byte field.

sections.title: MPPC Packets
sections.content:
Before any MPPC packets may be communicated, PPP must reach the Network-Layer Protocol phase and the CCP Control Protocol must reach the Opened state. Exactly one MPPC datagram is encapsulated in the PPP Information field, and the PPP Protocol field indicates type hex 00FD for all compressed datagrams. The maximum length of the MPPC datagram sent over a PPP link is the same as the maximum length of the Information field of a PPP encapsulated packet, and since the history buffer is limited to 8192 bytes, this length cannot be greater than 8192 bytes. Only packets with PPP Protocol numbers in the range hex 0021 to hex 00FA are compressed; other packets are not passed through the MPPC processor and are sent with their original PPP Protocol numbers.

Padding is not recommended with MPPC, since it defeats the purpose of compression. If the sender must use padding, it must negotiate the Self-Describing-Padding Configuration option during the LCP phase and use self-describing pads.

MPPC does not require a reliable link. Instead it relies on a 12 bit coherency count in each packet to keep the history buffers synchronized. If the receiver recognizes that the coherency count received in the packet does not match the count it is expecting, it sends a CCP Reset-Request packet to resynchronize its history buffer with the sender's history buffer. MPPC expects the packets to be delivered in sequence, otherwise history buffer resynchronization will not occur. It may be used over a reliable link as described in PPP Reliable Transmission, but that typically just adds unnecessary overhead, since only the coherency count is required.

If compressing the data results in data expansion, the original data is sent as an uncompressed MPPC packet. The sender must flush the history before compressing any more data and set the FLUSHED bit on the next outgoing packet.
sections.plainLanguage: Every compressed packet carries a counter that goes up by one each time. If the receiver's counter and the sender's counter no longer agree, one packet has been lost and the two ends have to start their history again.

sections.title: Packet Format
sections.content:
The packet format is a PPP Protocol field, then four flag bits and a 12 bit coherency count, then the compressed data. The PPP Protocol field is 00FD once the protocol has been negotiated, and that value may be compressed when Protocol-Field-Compression is negotiated.

Bit A, the FLUSHED bit, indicates that the history buffer has just been initialized before the packet was generated, so the packet can always be decompressed because it is not based on any previous history. It is typically sent to inform the peer that the sender has initialized its history buffer before compressing the packet and that the receiving peer must initialize its history buffer before decompressing the packet. Compression and decompression histories are always initialized with all zeroes.

Bit B indicates that the packet was moved to the front of the history buffer, typically because there was no room at the end. It tells the decompressor to set its history pointer to the beginning of the buffer. The memo notes that this bit must be set at least once for every 8192 bytes of data that is sent compressed, and that it may also be set even if the sender's history buffer is not full. Initialized history that has not been used for compressing data must not be referred to in the compressed packets. Bit C indicates that the packet is compressed, and Bit D must be set to 0.

The coherency count is used to assure that the packets are sent in proper order and that no packet has been dropped. It starts at 0, is always increased by 1, and never decreases or goes back; when all bits are 1, the count returns to 0. The compressed data begins with the protocol field, so for an IP packet the compressor first tries to compress the 0021 protocol field and then compresses the IP header. If the packet contains header compression, the MPPC compressor is applied after the header compression has been performed, and must be applied to the compressed header as well.
sections.plainLanguage: Four bits in the header carry the small messages the two ends need: one says the history has just been thrown away, one says the packet wrapped round the history buffer, and one says whether the data is compressed.

sections.title: The Compressor and Its Encoding
sections.content:
The compressor runs through the length of the frame producing as output either a Literal, a byte to be sent uncompressed, or a Copy tuple of an Offset and a Length-of-Match. The Offset is the number of bytes back in the history where the match lies, and the Length-of-Match is the number of bytes to copy from that location. The memo's example is the string "for whom the bell tolls, the bell tolls for thee.", which the compressor produces as "for whom the bell tolls,<16,15> <40,4><19,3>e."

A Literal is a byte sent uncompressed. If its value is below hex 80 it is encoded with its value itself; if it is greater than hex 7F it is sent as bits 10 followed by the lower 7 bits of the literal. So literal hex 56 is transmitted as 01010110 and literal hex E7 as 101100111.

A Copy tuple has two elements, the Offset and the Length-of-Match, and the Offset is encoded before the Length-of-Match. Offset values less than 64 are encoded as bits 1111 followed by the lower 6 bits of the value; values between 64 and 320 as bits 1110 followed by the lower 8 bits of the value minus 64; and values between 320 and 8191 as bits 110 followed by the lower 13 bits of the value minus 320. So offset 3 is encoded as 1111 000011, offset 128 as 1110 01000000 and offset 1024 as 110 0001011000000.

Length-of-Match values are encoded with a run of ones as a prefix followed by the remaining bits. A length of 3 is encoded with bit 0; values from 4 to 7 as 10 followed by the lower 2 bits; from 8 to 15 as 110 followed by the lower 3 bits; from 16 to 31 as 1110 followed by the lower 4 bits; from 32 to 63 as 11110 followed by the lower 5 bits; and so on, up to lengths between 4096 and 8191 as 111111111110 followed by the lower 12 bits. The largest length that can be encoded is 8191. So length 15 is encoded as 110 111, length 120 as 111110 111000 and length 4097 as 111111111110 000000000001.
sections.plainLanguage: The compressor emits only two kinds of thing: a byte to copy literally, or a pair giving how far back to look and how many bytes to take. The pair is packed into bits so that common values take few bits.

sections.title: Synchronization
sections.content:
Packets may be lost during transfer. If the coherency count maintained by the decompressor does not match the coherency count received in the compressed packet, the decompressor drops the packet and sends a CCP Reset-Request packet. The compressor, on receiving this packet, flushes the history buffer and sets the FLUSHED bit in the next packet it sends. The decompressor, on receiving a packet with the FLUSHED bit set, flushes its history buffer and sets its coherency count to the one transmitted by the compressor in that packet. Synchronization is therefore achieved without a CCP Reset-Ack packet.

The Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed in this memo.
sections.plainLanguage: When the counters stop matching, the receiver drops the packet and asks the sender to start again. The sender marks its next packet so the receiver knows to throw its history away too.

fields.name: PPP Protocol
fields.desc: Set to the compressed datagram value once CCP has negotiated the protocol.

fields.name: Flags A B C D
fields.desc: A is FLUSHED, B says the packet moved to the front of the history buffer, C says the packet is compressed, and D must be 0.

fields.name: Coherency Count
fields.desc: Counts up by one for every packet, so the two ends can spot a lost one.

fields.name: Compressed Data
fields.desc: The compressed protocol field followed by the compressed data.

items.title: Literal above hex 7F
items.text: Sent as bits 10 followed by the lower 7 bits of the literal.

items.title: Offset below 64
items.text: Bits 1111 followed by the lower 6 bits of the value.

items.title: Offset from 64 to 320
items.text: Bits 1110 followed by the lower 8 bits of the value minus 64.

items.title: Offset from 320 to 8191
items.text: Bits 110 followed by the lower 13 bits of the value minus 320.

items.title: Length of match
items.text: A run of ones as a prefix, from bit 0 for a length of 3 up to twelve ones for lengths of 4096 to 8191.
